claims.text: A local mixture of many principal elements in a high-entropy alloy produces lattice distortions.
Chemically induced lattice distortions act as intrinsic dislocation-pinning sites.
Lattice-distortion pinning slows dislocation motion during high-strain-rate loading.
Dislocation pinning delays dynamic recovery by temporarily trapping dislocations.
Delayed dynamic recovery elevates dynamic yield strength.
Delayed dynamic recovery increases strain hardening.
Distributed and gradual release of pinned dislocations preserves sufficient plasticity and ductility.
Relative to a conventional alloy matched in initial yield strength and grain size, the HEA will have higher dynamic yield strength.
Relative to the matched conventional alloy, the HEA will have a steeper strain-hardening rate under high-strain-rate loading.
Post-loading microscopy will show a higher density of pinned dislocations in the HEA than in the baseline alloy.
Diffraction or microscopy will show more heterogeneous local lattice strains in the HEA than in the baseline alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies to well-mixed, disordered HEA solid solutions.
Ordered phases or significant precipitation may make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
The proposed mechanism may cease to dominate at very high temperatures where diffusion-induced processes dominate plastic behavior.
Twinning or phase instability may also contribute to the dynamic mechanical response.
A controlled comparison should match the HEA and baseline alloy in grain size and initial yield strength while varying chemical disorder.
